back: A tax on spending on goods and services, collected from sellers and partly passed on to consumers in higher prices (for example VAT, excise duty).

front: Specific tax versus ad valorem tax?
back: Specific: a fixed amount per unit. Ad valorem: a percentage of the price (for example VAT).
A government payment to producers (or consumers) that lowers costs and price and raises output and consumption.

front: How does an indirect tax change the market?
back: Supply shifts left (up by the tax): price rises, quantity falls.

front: How does a subsidy change the market?
back: Supply shifts right (down by the subsidy): price falls, quantity rises.

front: How do you calculate tax revenue and subsidy cost?
back: Tax revenue = tax per unit × new quantity. Subsidy cost = subsidy per unit × new quantity.

front: Who bears most of an indirect tax when demand is inelastic?
back: Consumers: sellers can pass most of the tax on because buyers keep buying.

front: What shape is the shift caused by an ad valorem tax?
back: The new supply curve is steeper (it pivots), because the tax per unit rises with price.

front: Give two disadvantages of indirect taxes on demerit goods.
back: Little effect when demand is inelastic; regressive; encourage smuggling; hard to set the right rate.
Opportunity cost / higher taxes; firms may become inefficient and dependent; hard to remove; may not be fully passed on.
